screens.title: Getting Started with the Unity Editor
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll prepare your development environment and become fluent with the Unity Editor's essential windows and building blocks. First, we'll describe why Unity Hub matters: it centrally manages multiple Editor versions and project installations so you can match toolchains across assignments. Then we walk through creating a new project and choosing a 3D or 2D template based on the game's needs. You'll also see how the Editor is organized into productive work areas—Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector—each serving a specific purpose when building your world. We'll define GameObjects and Components, explain why every GameObject must have a Transform, and show how components make objects visible, physical, and interactive. Finally, you'll perform a simple hands-on activity: create common primitives, manipulate them with Move, Rotate, and Scale tools, and save a scene. This orientation matters because a clean setup and an understanding of the Editor windows prevents wasted time later. As you begin, remember that a GameObject is an empty container until components are attached; this distinction is the core mental model that will guide your work. Are you ready to set up and explore?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Getting Started with the Unity Editor
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Getting Started with the Unity Editor

Install Unity Hub, pick the right Editor modules, create a 3D project, and learn the five primary Editor windows plus the GameObject–Component model.

Install
Get Unity Hub, then use it to install the Editor with needed build modules.
Create
Start a new 3D or 2D Core project with a clear name and folder location.
Explore
Open Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project and Inspector to learn their roles.
In this lesson
Install Hub and an Editor version with modules, create a 3D Core project, add primitives, practice transform tools, and save your first scene.
Concept Map
Hub → Editor → Project → Scene (GameObjects + Components)
Unity Hub: central manager for Editor versions and projects
Editor windows: Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, Inspector
GameObject + Component: the composition model for behavior and visuals
Quick Tip
Install common build modules now — skipping build support often stops later deployment. Use descriptive project names to keep work organized.

screens.title: What you'll learn
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the first hands-on steps with Unity. You'll first learn to install Unity Hub and an Editor version with the necessary build modules so that your projects can be built for desktop, mobile, or web. This matters because skipping modules creates blocker errors later when you try to export. Next you'll practice navigating the Editor's primary windows—Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector—and learn what each window controls so you can efficiently author scenes. Third, you'll create a new project and make a deliberate choice between 2D and 3D templates; the 3D Core template configures cameras and lighting for three-dimensional games while 2D Core uses orthographic projection and sprite-friendly defaults. Finally, you'll master the GameObject and Component relation and manipulate primitives through the Transform component and transform tools. Each objective includes a short practical action: install modules, open and identify windows, start a new 3D project, and create and transform a cube. These skills prevent common beginner errors and give you a repeatable workflow for every project you build.

screens.title: How these skills help you
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives are practical: installing the right Editor modules prevents platform build failures, which saves time when you want to test on desktop, mobile, or web. Knowing the Editor windows lets you move between authoring and previewing quickly; the Scene view is for construction while the Game view shows the player's camera output. Choosing 2D or 3D at project creation matters because it sets camera projection, physics defaults, and rendering behavior—changing templates later is possible but requires extra configuration. Understanding GameObjects and Components is the central mental model: a GameObject alone has only spatial information from its Transform, while behavior and appearance come from components like Mesh Renderer, Rigidbody, and custom scripts. During the lab, practice creating primitives, changing Transform values, and using Move, Rotate, and Scale tools so these actions become second nature. A common beginner mistake is to skip build support modules and then be unable to export; another is to expect a GameObject to be visible without a Mesh Renderer. Keep these checks in mind as you work.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Learning Objectives

How these skills help you

Concrete outcomes to achieve in the lab and key mistakes to avoid.

Practical Outcome
Be able to open Unity Hub, install an Editor with build modules, and create a named 3D project ready for development.
Editor Fluency
Move smoothly between Scene and Game views, and use the Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector to organize assets and edit properties.
Common Mistakes
Skipping build modules or assuming a GameObject is visible without a Mesh Renderer are frequent blockers beginners face.
Lab Checkpoint

screens.title: Install Unity Hub and the Editor
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Unity Hub and the Editor is a small process with a big payoff. Start by installing Unity Hub, the central manager for your Editor versions and projects. Use Hub to add a recommended Editor release, and when the installer prompts you, select the build support modules that match targets you'll use. For this specialization choose desktop build support for your OS, Android build support, WebGL build support, and the Documentation module for offline reference. A clear reason to select these now is to avoid later errors when exporting builds. For example, if you skip Android support and then try to deploy to a phone, the build will fail until you install that module. The practical steps are: open Hub, pick Install Editor, choose modules, and wait for the download and install to finish. After installation, verify the Editor appears in Hub's Installs list and that you can open it. A common misconception is that a default Editor will always include every platform; it will not. Takeaway: installing correct modules upfront saves hours and keeps your project portable across devices. Do this before creating your first project.

keyIdea.title: Install Flow
keyIdea.text: Use Unity Hub to add an Editor and choose build support modules for the platforms you plan to target.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Install Unity Hub
Step-by-step
1. Install Unity Hub
Run the Hub installer for your operating system and sign in if needed. Hub manages versions and projects centrally.
2. Add an Editor
Use Hub's Installs panel to add a recommended Editor release for this course.
3. Select Modules
Choose desktop build support for your OS, Android, WebGL, and Documentation for offline help.
4. Verify Install
Confirm the Editor appears in Hub and can be launched.
Why modules matter
Build support modules add platform-specific tooling and SDKs. Without them, export attempts will fail with missing platform tools.
Concrete Example
If you plan to publish to Android but skip Android Build Support, the Editor will not find the Android SDK and the Android build will fail until you add the module.
Common Mistake
Assuming an Editor install includes every target platform. Always verify and add modules now to avoid later build errors.

screens.title: Choose between 2D and 3D templates
screens.narratorSegment: When you create a new project in Unity Hub you choose a template—commonly 3D Core or 2D Core for this course. Templates matter because they set camera projection, physics defaults, and essential settings that affect workflow. The 3D Core template opens with a perspective camera, lighting configured for 3D materials, and 3D physics. It's the right choice for platformers, first-person games, or any project where depth and perspective are needed. The 2D Core template configures an orthographic camera, 2D sprite rendering, and 2D physics settings such as Box Collider 2D. Pick 2D for side-scrollers or top-down tile games where sprites and 2D colliders are the primary workflow. A useful concrete example: starting a pixel-art platformer in 3D will force you to adjust the camera and physics to match 2D behavior; this wastes time. Conversely, a 3D racing game in 2D template will lack depth and proper rendering. Misconception: templates are not permanent locks; you can change settings later, but choosing correctly up front saves configuration work. Takeaway: pick the template that matches your game's spatial needs to keep defaults aligned with your design.

keyIdea.title: Template Choice
keyIdea.text: Choose 3D Core for perspective, lighting, and 3D physics; choose 2D Core for orthographic cameras and 2D sprite workflows.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › 2D vs 3D Templates
3D Core
Perspective camera, 3D lighting, 3D physics
Ideal when depth, perspective, and 3D modeling are central. Includes default camera and lighting tuned for three-dimensional scenes.
Example
A first-person or third-person game that relies on depth and 3D collisions should use 3D Core.
2D Core
Orthographic camera, sprite renderer, 2D physics
Use when your game is built from sprites and 2D colliders, such as tile-based or side-scrolling games where orthographic projection is desired.
Example
A pixel-art platformer benefits from the 2D template because colliders and camera behavior match 2D expectations.
Misconception
Templates are not irreversible, but changing major settings later requires extra configuration. Choose to save time and reduce friction.

screens.title: The Editor's primary windows
screens.narratorSegment: The Unity Editor organizes your work into windows that each solve a specific problem. The Scene view is your visual construction area where you arrange and edit GameObjects; think of it like a 3D canvas. The Game view is a preview from the active camera—it's what the player will actually see. The Hierarchy lists every GameObject in the current scene and shows parent-child relationships, which control relative transforms and grouping. The Project window is an asset browser: models, textures, scripts, and audio live here and can be dragged into the scene. The Inspector shows the properties of the currently selected object or asset, and it's the place where you add and configure Components. Understanding how these windows work together is critical: you drag assets from Project into the Scene or Hierarchy, select an object to tune its Components in the Inspector, then preview the results in the Game view. A common misconception is treating the Scene view as the final output; always check the Game view for what the player will experience. Example: place a light in Scene, then use the Game view to ensure shadows and camera framing look correct. Takeaway: learning these relationships makes editing deliberate and efficient.

keyIdea.title: Window Roles
keyIdea.text: Scene edits build the world, Game previews the player view, Hierarchy organizes objects, Project stores assets, Inspector edits components and properties.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Editor Windows
Editor relationships
Scene View
Arrange GameObjects and build levels interactively; navigation uses orbit, pan, and zoom.
Game View
Preview the active camera output to check what players will see at runtime.
Hierarchy
Lists scene GameObjects and their parent-child relationships for organization.
Project
Asset browser containing models, textures, scripts, and audio for your project.
Inspector
Edit selected object's Components and properties. Add or remove Components here to change behavior and appearance.
Concrete Example
Drag a model from Project into Scene, group it under a parent in Hierarchy, select it and edit materials or Rigidbody settings in the Inspector, and then test in Game view to confirm the player camera frames the object as intended.
Misconception
Scene edits are not the final output. Always validate changes in the Game view because camera and player experience may differ from the Scene perspective.

screens.title: Scene navigation and transform tools
screens.narratorSegment: Learning to move around the Scene view and use the transform tools is essential. Navigation controls let you inspect objects from any angle: orbit with right-click and mouse movement, pan with middle-click and drag, and zoom with the scroll wheel. Once you can move the camera comfortably, use the transform tools to edit objects: the Move Tool lets you drag along X, Y, and Z axes; the Rotate Tool rotates around local or global axes; the Scale Tool resizes objects; and the Rect Tool is used for 2D UI layout. Every GameObject must have a Transform component containing position, rotation, and scale fields. As you drag objects in the Scene, observe the Inspector—these Transform values update numerically in real time. A concrete exercise: create a Cube, click it, press W to enable Move, then drag the X handle and watch the X position change in the Inspector. A common mistake is unintentionally placing objects far from the origin; use reset or set values to zero if needed. Takeaway: combine visual tools and numeric values to place objects precisely and avoid accidental transforms that break your layout.

keyIdea.title: Transform Practice
keyIdea.text: Use navigation and transform tools alongside the Inspector values to position, rotate, and scale objects precisely and recover from accidental transforms.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Scene Navigation
Navigation Controls
  • Orbit scene camera: right-click + drag to change view angle.
  • Pan: middle-click + drag to move the camera without rotating.
  • Zoom: scroll wheel to approach or retreat from an object.
Transform Tools
  • Move Tool (W): drag axis handles to move objects along X, Y, Z.
  • Rotate Tool (E): rotate by angle and watch rotation values in Inspector.
  • Scale Tool (R): change object size uniformly or per axis.
Guided Exercise
Create a Cube, press W, drag the X handle while watching the Transform X value in the Inspector. Press E to rotate and R to scale. Practice resetting transforms when needed by zeroing position values.
Mistake to avoid
Accidentally moving objects far from the origin. Use the Inspector to set precise numbers or undo to revert unexpected changes.

screens.title: GameObjects and Components
screens.narratorSegment: GameObjects and Components form Unity's core composition model. Define a GameObject as an empty container that holds a Transform and can be given behavior by attaching Components. The Transform provides position, rotation, and scale—always present and required. Components are modular pieces that add rendering, physics, input handling, and scripting. For example, a Cube primitive typically includes a Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, and a Box Collider. To enable physics simulation you add a Rigidbody component. To add custom behavior you attach a script component. A concrete example: to make a visible, physical cube that falls under gravity you create a Cube GameObject, confirm it has a Mesh Renderer and Box Collider, then add a Rigidbody. Without the Rigidbody it will sit static even though it has a collider. A common misconception is expecting a GameObject to have functionality by default; it must have the appropriate components to act. Takeaway: think in terms of composition—start with a transform, then add the minimal components needed for visibility, interaction, and behavior. GameObjects and Components means gameobjects are containers; components add visuals and behavior. the transform is mandatory and every other feature is component-driven.. In practical terms, the composition model that makes objects functional. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › GameObjects & Components
Definition
A GameObject is an entity with a Transform; Components are attachable modules that add behavior and visuals.
Core Components on a Cube
  • Transform — position, rotation, scale (required)
  • Mesh Filter — defines the mesh geometry
  • Mesh Renderer — makes the mesh visible
  • Box Collider — collision shape for physics and overlaps
Concrete Scenario
Create a Cube, add a Rigidbody to enable gravity. Without Rigidbody the cube's collider will detect collisions but it will not move under physics.
Takeaway
Components give GameObjects functionality. Attach only what you need and inspect values in the Inspector to tune behavior.

screens.title: Create primitives and manipulate them
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through creating simple GameObjects and practicing transforms. In the Hierarchy, right-click and choose 3D Object → Cube. The Cube appears in the Scene and the Hierarchy and will show its components in the Inspector. Repeat to add a Sphere and a Cylinder. Use the Move Tool to place the objects so they form a simple structure—an example is arranging them like a snowman: Sphere on top of Cylinder, Cube as a hat. While moving and rotating, watch the Transform values update in the Inspector; this feedback builds confidence in precise placement. Next, use the Rotate Tool to angle the Cylinder and the Scale Tool to adjust the Cube hat. Save your work using File > Save Scene and name it MyFirstScene. A common beginner error is accidentally nesting objects under unexpected parents in the Hierarchy; review parent-child relationships because children inherit parent transforms. Takeaway: practice these steps until placing, rotating, and scaling feel intuitive, and save frequently to avoid losing progress. keyIdea.title: Practical Lab
keyIdea.text: Create primitives, use transform tools to arrange them into a simple composition, and save your scene as MyFirstScene.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Create & Manipulate
Steps
  1. Create a Cube (Hierarchy → 3D Object → Cube).
  2. Create a Sphere and Cylinder the same way.
  3. Use Move (W), Rotate (E), Scale (R) to position objects into a simple structure.
  4. Save scene as MyFirstScene in the Assets folder.
Scenario
Arrange Sphere atop Cylinder and place Cube as a hat. Use numeric values in the Inspector to align objects precisely when snapping visually is difficult.
Common Mistake
Accidentally parenting objects under another object. Check the Hierarchy to confirm intended parent-child relationships.

screens.title: Project Window and asset management
screens.narratorSegment: The Project window is your project's asset library and functions like a game-specific file system. Assets such as models, textures, audio, and scripts are stored here and can be imported or created inside the Assets folder. You drag assets from the Project window into the Scene to instantiate them as GameObjects or into the Hierarchy for organized placement. Importantly, assets in Project are reusable: a single model asset can be placed multiple times into a scene or into other scenes without duplicating the file. A concrete example: import a tree model into Project, then drag it into Scene three times to create a grove; each instance references the same asset. A common mistake is editing an instantiated object's properties and assuming the source asset changes; by default instances reference the asset, but component changes apply to the instance unless you explicitly modify the asset or use prefab workflows. Takeaway: use the Project window to manage and reuse assets, and rely on the Hierarchy and Scene for placement and composition. In practical terms, how assets live and move between project, hierarchy, and scene. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Scene vs Game view: authoring vs player view
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between Scene and Game views helps you author confidently. It provides navigation controls and non-player visuals like handles and gizmos for editing. Takeaway: author in Scene, validate in Game—this separation reduces surprises when testing your level or camera framing. screens.title: Save, organize, and avoid beginner pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Good project hygiene reduces friction as a project grows. Save your scene early and often—File > Save Scene or Ctrl+S/Cmd+S—and give descriptive names such as MyFirstScene. Organize assets into folders inside the Project window (Textures, Models, Scripts) to find resources quickly. When placing objects, check the Hierarchy for unintended parenting; children inherit transforms from their parents which can lead to surprising positions or scales. When experimenting, use Undo to revert accidental changes, and if an object ends up far from the origin, zero out its Transform values or re-parent it carefully. Another common pitfall is neglecting build modules during Editor install—confirm required modules are present in Hub before starting heavy work. Finally, use version control or regular backups if possible; repeated saves are helpful but do not replace commits. Concrete action: after arranging your three primitives, save the scene and create folders in Project to hold any assets you import. Takeaway: small organizational habits prevent hours of cleanup later and keep your scenes predictable and maintainable. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll prepare your development environment and become fluent with the Unity Editor's essential windows and building blocks. First, we'll describe why Unity Hub matters: it centrally manages multiple Editor versions and project installations so you can match toolchains across assignments. Then we walk through creating a new project and choosing a 3D or 2D template based on the game's needs. You'll also see how the Editor is organized into productive work areas—Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector—each serving a specific purpose when building your world. We'll define GameObjects and Components, explain why every GameObject must have a Transform, and show how components make objects visible, physical, and interactive. Finally, you'll perform a simple hands-on activity: create common primitives, manipulate them with Move, Rotate, and Scale tools, and save a scene. This orientation matters because a clean setup and an understanding of the Editor windows prevents wasted time later. As you begin, remember that a GameObject is an empty container until components are attached; this distinction is the core mental model that will guide your work. Are you ready to set up and explore?

These objectives guide the first hands-on steps with Unity. You'll first learn to install Unity Hub and an Editor version with the necessary build modules so that your projects can be built for desktop, mobile, or web. This matters because skipping modules creates blocker errors later when you try to export. Next you'll practice navigating the Editor's primary windows—Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector—and learn what each window controls so you can efficiently author scenes. Third, you'll create a new project and make a deliberate choice between 2D and 3D templates; the 3D Core template configures cameras and lighting for three-dimensional games while 2D Core uses orthographic projection and sprite-friendly defaults. Finally, you'll master the GameObject and Component relation and manipulate primitives through the Transform component and transform tools. Each objective includes a short practical action: install modules, open and identify windows, start a new 3D project, and create and transform a cube. These skills prevent common beginner errors and give you a repeatable workflow for every project you build.

These objectives are practical: installing the right Editor modules prevents platform build failures, which saves time when you want to test on desktop, mobile, or web. Knowing the Editor windows lets you move between authoring and previewing quickly; the Scene view is for construction while the Game view shows the player's camera output. Choosing 2D or 3D at project creation matters because it sets camera projection, physics defaults, and rendering behavior—changing templates later is possible but requires extra configuration. Understanding GameObjects and Components is the central mental model: a GameObject alone has only spatial information from its Transform, while behavior and appearance come from components like Mesh Renderer, Rigidbody, and custom scripts. During the lab, practice creating primitives, changing Transform values, and using Move, Rotate, and Scale tools so these actions become second nature. A common beginner mistake is to skip build support modules and then be unable to export; another is to expect a GameObject to be visible without a Mesh Renderer. Keep these checks in mind as you work.

Installing Unity Hub and the Editor is a small process with a big payoff. Start by installing Unity Hub, the central manager for your Editor versions and projects. Use Hub to add a recommended Editor release, and when the installer prompts you, select the build support modules that match targets you'll use. For this specialization choose desktop build support for your OS, Android build support, WebGL build support, and the Documentation module for offline reference. A clear reason to select these now is to avoid later errors when exporting builds. For example, if you skip Android support and then try to deploy to a phone, the build will fail until you install that module. The practical steps are: open Hub, pick Install Editor, choose modules, and wait for the download and install to finish. After installation, verify the Editor appears in Hub's Installs list and that you can open it. A common misconception is that a default Editor will always include every platform; it will not. Takeaway: installing correct modules upfront saves hours and keeps your project portable across devices. Do this before creating your first project.

When you create a new project in Unity Hub you choose a template—commonly 3D Core or 2D Core for this course. Templates matter because they set camera projection, physics defaults, and essential settings that affect workflow. The 3D Core template opens with a perspective camera, lighting configured for 3D materials, and 3D physics. It's the right choice for platformers, first-person games, or any project where depth and perspective are needed. The 2D Core template configures an orthographic camera, 2D sprite rendering, and 2D physics settings such as Box Collider 2D. Pick 2D for side-scrollers or top-down tile games where sprites and 2D colliders are the primary workflow. A useful concrete example: starting a pixel-art platformer in 3D will force you to adjust the camera and physics to match 2D behavior; this wastes time. Conversely, a 3D racing game in 2D template will lack depth and proper rendering. Misconception: templates are not permanent locks; you can change settings later, but choosing correctly up front saves configuration work. Takeaway: pick the template that matches your game's spatial needs to keep defaults aligned with your design.

The Unity Editor organizes your work into windows that each solve a specific problem. The Scene view is your visual construction area where you arrange and edit GameObjects; think of it like a 3D canvas. The Game view is a preview from the active camera—it's what the player will actually see. The Hierarchy lists every GameObject in the current scene and shows parent-child relationships, which control relative transforms and grouping. The Project window is an asset browser: models, textures, scripts, and audio live here and can be dragged into the scene. The Inspector shows the properties of the currently selected object or asset, and it's the place where you add and configure Components. Understanding how these windows work together is critical: you drag assets from Project into the Scene or Hierarchy, select an object to tune its Components in the Inspector, then preview the results in the Game view. A common misconception is treating the Scene view as the final output; always check the Game view for what the player will experience. Example: place a light in Scene, then use the Game view to ensure shadows and camera framing look correct. Takeaway: learning these relationships makes editing deliberate and efficient.

Learning to move around the Scene view and use the transform tools is essential. Navigation controls let you inspect objects from any angle: orbit with right-click and mouse movement, pan with middle-click and drag, and zoom with the scroll wheel. Once you can move the camera comfortably, use the transform tools to edit objects: the Move Tool lets you drag along X, Y, and Z axes; the Rotate Tool rotates around local or global axes; the Scale Tool resizes objects; and the Rect Tool is used for 2D UI layout. Every GameObject must have a Transform component containing position, rotation, and scale fields. As you drag objects in the Scene, observe the Inspector—these Transform values update numerically in real time. A concrete exercise: create a Cube, click it, press W to enable Move, then drag the X handle and watch the X position change in the Inspector. A common mistake is unintentionally placing objects far from the origin; use reset or set values to zero if needed. GameObjects and Components form Unity's core composition model. Define a GameObject as an empty container that holds a Transform and can be given behavior by attaching Components. For example, a Cube primitive typically includes a Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, and a Box Collider. To enable physics simulation you add a Rigidbody component. To add custom behavior you attach a script component. Without the Rigidbody it will sit static even though it has a collider. A common misconception is expecting a GameObject to have functionality by default; it must have the appropriate components to act. Takeaway: think in terms of composition—start with a transform, then add the minimal components needed for visibility, interaction, and behavior.
